bib.title: Pure Exploration (Chapter 33 of Bandit Algorithms)
bib.venue: Bandit Algorithms, Cambridge University Press (book chapter, pp. 403-420)

read.skipped: None. Year 2020 is the book's publication year, not printed in the chapter text.

question: How should a bandit learner explore when only the final recommendation matters (no cost for exploring), under simple regret, fixed-confidence and fixed-budget best-arm identification?
contributions: Simple regret analysis of uniform exploration and its reduction from cumulative-regret policies
Fixed-confidence BAI: instance lower bound c*(nu) log(1/4delta), and track-and-stop matching it asymptotically
Fixed-budget BAI: sequential halving bound with H2 and comparison against uniform exploration

results.claim: Sequential halving's error probability is bounded by 3 log2(k) exp(-n/(16 H2 log2 k)), with H2 = max_{i: gap>0} i/gap_i^2.
results.setup: Fixed budget n, k-armed 1-subgaussian bandit, means sorted mu1>=...>=muk; theorem, not an experiment

results.claim: Track-and-stop is sound and its expected stopping time satisfies lim E[tau]/log(1/delta) = c*(nu) as delta -> 0, matching the lower bound.
results.setup: Unit-variance Gaussian k-armed bandits with a unique optimal arm; asymptotic in delta

results.claim: Any sound fixed-confidence learner needs E[tau] >= c*(nu) log(1/(4 delta)).
results.setup: Any class E of k-armed bandits, learner sound at confidence delta

results.claim: For two unit-variance Gaussian arms the constant is c*(nu)^-1 = (mu1-mu2)^2/8, with optimal allocation 1/2 each.
For Gaussian arms with variances sigma_i^2 and k=2, c* = 2(sigma1+sigma2)^2/gap2^2.
results.setup: k=2 Gaussian bandits with known variances (Exercise 33.4)

results.claim: Uniform exploration simple regret is bounded by min over Delta of Delta + sum_{i: gap_i>Delta} gap_i exp(-floor(n/k) gap_i^2/4).
Worst-case simple regret of uniform exploration is O(sqrt(k log k / n)); the log k is tight for UE.
Minimax simple regret over k-armed bandits is O(sqrt(k/n)), obtained by recommending an arm drawn from a cumulative-regret policy's empirical play distribution: simple regret = R_n / n.
results.setup: Reduction from any cumulative-regret policy (Proposition 33.2, Corollary 33.3); lower bound C sqrt(k/n) is Exercise 33.1

results.claim: Cumulative-regret-optimal algorithms are poor for best-arm identification: the probability of picking a suboptimal arm decays only polynomially in n (liminf of -log P/log n <= 1+eps on some instance).
results.setup: Asymptotically optimal cumulative-regret policy on Gaussian bandits (Note 2, Exercise 33.5, due to Bubeck et al. 2009)

results.claim: H2 <= H1 <= (1+log k) H2, both inequalities essentially tight, where H1 = sum_i min{1/gap_i^2, 1/gap_min^2}.

When all gaps equal, H2 = k/Delta^2; sequential halving exponent is Theta(n Delta^2/(k log k)) vs Theta(n Delta^2/k) for UE, so UE is moderately better. When one arm has small gap Delta and all others gap 1, H2 = Theta(1/Delta^2) and SH exponent Theta(n Delta^2) vs UE Theta(n Delta^2/k), so SH is significantly better.
results.setup: Fixed budget n; equal-gap instance vs one-hard-arm instance

results.claim: Track-and-stop threshold: beta_t(delta) = k log(t^2+t) + f^-1(delta), roughly 2k log t + log(1/delta), improvable to roughly k log log t + log(1/delta) with an LIL bound.
results.setup: Unit-variance Gaussian bandits, stopping rule Z_t >= beta_t(delta)
results.note: Quoted ligature-free; text also says beta ~ 2k log t + log(1/delta)

results.claim: Track-and-stop forces exploration of any arm with fewer than sqrt(t) pulls; the authors say there is nothing fundamental about sqrt(t) and no principled way to tune it is known.
Authors question the practicality of exact best-arm identification: any suboptimal arm with small enough gap relative to the budget is acceptable, which simple regret captures better.
results.quote: makes us question the practicality of the setting

limits: Fixed-confidence optimality is asymptotic (delta -> 0); finite-time upper bounds matching the finite-time lower bound are an open question (Note 7).
Track-and-stop is analysed for unit-variance Gaussian arms only; forced-exploration rate and beta_t(delta) are not tuned in a principled way (Notes 7, 8).
Fixed-budget setting has no asymptotically matching upper and lower bounds; sequential halving is only 'roughly optimal'.
Chapter has no experiments and no empirical figures; everything is theorem and proof.

Chapter does not cover successive elimination, LUCB or lil'UCB; only uniform exploration, track-and-stop and sequential halving are given as algorithms (elimination is mentioned only in the hint to Exercise 33.11).
Instance-dependent upper and lower bounds on simple regret are unstudied (Note 9).
practices: Use a pure-exploration algorithm, not a cumulative-regret one, when exploration is free: UCB-style policies play suboptimal arms too rarely, giving only polynomial decay of error (p.405, Note 2).
Under a fixed budget with heterogeneous gaps prefer sequential halving over uniform exploration; with equal gaps uniform exploration is moderately better (p.413).
Do not use empirical means from a cumulative-regret run as unbiased estimates: they tend to be negatively biased (Note 3, p.414).
Use simple regret rather than exact identification as the criterion when any small-gap arm is acceptable (Note 5, p.414).
For fixed confidence, sample arms in proportion to the optimal allocation alpha*(nu) and stop when the generalised likelihood ratio Z_t exceeds beta_t(delta) (Algorithm 21, p.410).

terms.definition: Problems where there is no price to be paid for exploring; the learner is judged on a final recommendation
R_n^simple(pi,nu) = E[Delta_{A_{n+1}}(nu)], the expected gap of the arm recommended in round n+1
Variant of pure exploration where the learner is rewarded only for identifying an exactly optimal arm
Given delta in (0,1), output an optimal arm with probability at least 1-delta using as few samples as possible; the stopping time tau is random
Given horizon n, minimise the probability that A_{n+1} is suboptimal
P(tau < inf and Delta_psi(nu) > 0) <= delta for all nu in E
The F_tau-measurable function psi in [k] giving the recommended action
Instance constant with c*(nu)^-1 = sup_alpha inf_{nu' in E_alt(nu)} sum_i alpha_i D(nu_i, nu'_i)
Policy that plays the arm maximising t*alpha_hat_i(t) - T_i(t), with forced exploration of arms below sqrt(t) pulls, and stops when Z_t >= beta_t(delta)
Splits the budget into L=ceil(log2 k) phases, samples each surviving arm equally, then drops the bottom half
H1 = sum_i min{1/gap_i^2, 1/gap_min^2}; H2 = max_{i: gap_i>0} i/gap_i^2 (arms sorted by mean)
Find an epsilon-optimal arm with high probability using as few samples as possible
Finding an arm among the alpha*k arms with highest payoffs
Optimal computing budget allocation: the problem of finding an optimal sample allocation for Gaussian BAI (Chen et al. 2000)

code.snippet: for t=1..n: A_t = 1 + (t mod k); then A_{n+1} = argmax_i muhat_i(n)

choose each arm once, t=k; while Z_t < beta_t(delta): if argmin_i T_i(t) <= sqrt(t): A_{t+1}=argmin_i T_i(t) else A_{t+1}=argmax_i (t*alpha*_i(t) - T_i(t)); observe, update; return psi=i*(nuhat(t)), tau=t
L=ceil(log2 k), A_1=[k]; for l=1..L: T_l=floor(n/(L|A_l|)); pull each arm in A_l T_l times; muhat from last T_l samples; A_{l+1}=top ceil(|A_l|/2) arms; return the arm in A_{L+1}
